extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century polite society), particularly women and members of fashionable society
extracted.subtask_description: A set of prescriptive social, moral, and stylistic recommendations delivered as essays and letters in The Spectator (1711) about feminine conduct, reading choices, party behaviour, vanity, and language usage. The guidance is aimed at shaping manners, devotion, and public/private behaviour of polite society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize weightier considerations over secondary excellencies
rubrics_metrics.description: All that I contend for is, that those Excellencies, which are to be regarded but in the second Place, should not precede more weighty Considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let pleasures, distinctions, or minor excellences (beauty, amusement, social applause) take precedence over moral duties and more important considerations. The writer criticizes young women who delay serious life choices to pursue transient pleasures (music, plays, visiting) and urges attention to weightier moral concerns when making decisions (e.g., marriage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select devotional books that elevate the mind above the world
rubrics_metrics.description: When you are upon this Subject, choose Books which elevate the Mind above the World, and give a pleasing Indifference to little things in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer devotional writings that foster genuine elevation of heart and detachment from trivial concerns rather than short, sentimental 'weekly preparations' that encourage mechanical religion. The Hecatissa letter advises curating a female library with particular regard to books of devotion that produce inward change and disinterest in worldly vanities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical or performative devotion; make virtue inward
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of this I take to proceed from the Indiscretion of the Books themselves...they lead People of ordinary Capacities into great Errors, and raise in them a Mechanical Religion, entirely distinct from Morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular rituals, fixed hours of prayer, and perfunctory reading are insufficient if they do not touch the mind; avoid using devotion as a public show or a checklist. True virtue should be internalized — accompanied by pity for vice as well as contempt — rather than merely the absence of visible faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use devotion as a cover for vanity or vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The beauteous Philautia...has a very pretty furnished Closet...This is her Dressing-room, as well as Chapel; she has constantly before her a large Looking-glass, and upon the Table... 'Together lye her Prayer-book and Paint, At once t' improve the Sinner and the Saint'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid combining pious observance with ostentatious self-admiration; practices that mix prayer with vanity (glancing between mirror and prayerbook) indicate insincerity. The advice condemns using religion to justify or conceal indulgence in cards, fashion, or harsh behaviour toward others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the virtues proper to one's social role (female/domestic virtues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspire only to those Virtues that are peculiar to your Sex; follow your natural Modesty, and think it your greatest Commendation not to be talked of one way or other. Female Virtues are of a Domestick Turn. The Family is the proper Province for Private Women to shine in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women are urged to excel in domestic roles — modesty, motherhood, fidelity — rather than public partisan display. The essay invokes Pericles and Roman examples to recommend modest public behaviour and to valorize sacrifices for the common good rather than factional show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partisan public displays (the 'party patches')
rubrics_metrics.description: This way of declaring War upon one another...I found they were Patch'd differently...The Censorious say...the Patches turn to the Right or to the Left, according to the Principles of the Man who is most in Favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let political factionalism become a fashion or a public badge (literally patching the face to declare Whig or Tory). Such displays inflame hatreds, undermine feminine charms, and are inappropriate for those whose province is domestic virtue. The piece suggests civic-minded alternatives (e.g., sacrificing jewels to a public cause) instead of factional signalling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rivalry and vanity in beauty; prefer inward worth
rubrics_metrics.description: These two Rivals for the Reputation of Beauty...Their Nights grew restless with Meditation of new Dresses to outvie each other...Their Mothers...supported the several Pretensions of the Daughters with all that ill-chosen Sort of Expence...These Beginnings...improved into...an irreconcilable Hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competing for outward splendour and admirers leads to social ruin, hatred, and personal misery. The Brunetta/Phillis story shows how vanity and expenditure to outshine another produce tragic results; the implicit rule is to value inner qualities and avoid destructive competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose reading and leisure to cultivate the mind, not merely appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: I am Young, and very much inclin'd to follow the Paths of Innocence: but...I design to pass...in hearing Music, going to Plays, Visiting, and all other Satisfactions which Fortune and Youth, protected by Innocence and Virtue, can procure for... 'My Lover does not know I like him, therefore...I think to stay and know whether I may not like any one else better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leisure activities (theatre, music, visiting) should be balanced with inward cultivation; do not mistake innocent amusements for moral improvement. The writer wagers that such young women will change many affections and often choose poorly if guided mainly by sight and social display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct pronouns: 'who' for persons and 'which' for things; resist improper replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: That your Petitioners being in a forlorn...we have heard...these Words, 'That THAT that noble Lord urged'; which if one of us had had Justice done, would have sounded nobler thus, 'That WHO that noble Lord urged'. In the very Acts of Parliament...we find our selves often either not used, or used one instead of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition complains about the degradation of 'who' and 'which' in speech and law; the implied standard is careful, correct use of relative pronouns to preserve clarity and dignity in language. Examples include misuse in prayers and public oratory; this guidance defends grammatical propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sparing with expletives and filler 'that/this here', though rhetorically useful
rubrics_metrics.description: How can a judicious Man distinguish one thing from another, without saying 'This here', or 'That there'? And how can a sober Man without using the 'Expletives' of Oaths...make a Discourse of any tolerable Length, without 'That is'; and if he be a very grave Man indeed, without 'That is to say'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some conversational expletives ('that', 'this here', oaths) have rhetorical or conversational utility, excessive reliance on them is critiqued elsewhere in the piece; writers/speakers should balance natural speech with clarity and correctness, not allowing filler words to replace precise expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: True virtue is active, not merely the absence of wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: From hence I presume it arises that so many People call themselves Virtuous, from no other Pretence to it but an Absence of Ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morality should be measured by positive, inward dispositions and charitable behaviour rather than merely by not committing obvious sins. The writer recommends inward improvement and works that produce moral feeling, not just outward conformity to duties.
